asis-q3@run1.review_only: This comes from the [personalisation review](reviews/llm/personalization.md) and the notes on the two real-user studies; I did not reopen the papers.
asis-q3@run1.comment: Every number and page I checked matches the papers (54.6% and Fig. 5 on p. 8; 3.41–4.02 vs 3.18 and ρ ≤ 0.38 in Table 6, p. 15; r = 0.90; PRISM-X r = 0.98–0.99, τ 0.22/0.11 vs 0.57; SCV 0–19% in Table 3, p. 7; LaMP-QA 78%, p. 7; PersonaLens 0.78/0.52; 80 items and 367 ratings, p. 15). The answer says outright that it rests on a review and notes and was not checked in the papers; the PersonaLens point is also flagged as 'from a skim-level digest, no page'. The 'κ 0.31–0.43' range mixes Stage 3 (weighted κ 0.310) with Stage 2 (κ 0.426) without saying so. Point 4 is stated only as the mechanism (judges reward explicit mentions), without the human/GPT-5.4/Claude contrast. 'No paper in the library has users judge answers to their own questions over time' is borderline, since PRISM-X participants do rate responses in their own conversations; I did not count it because of the 'over time' qualifier.

asis-q3-r2.comment: All checked statements hold: Fig. 6 reading (open-weight judges reward mentions, humans and GPT-5.4 little sensitivity, Claude-S4.6 negative), Table 6 on p. 15, PRISM-X τ and r, PersonaLens Table 5 on p. 8 (0.52/0.75, 0.78/0.865, 100 dialogues), LaMP-QA 73%/58%/κ 0.726/78% on p. 7, Personalized Soups Tables 3–4 on p. 7 (P-Soups 55.23 under GPT-4, P-MORL 58.70 under humans), reward models about 0.3 on p. 9, inter-annotator 0.325/0.310 on p. 8, best judges 0.31–0.38. The skipped-paper claim is correct (catalog/skipped.yaml: arXiv 2406.11657, 2026-10-01, 'narrow'). The mention of the evaluation review is a how-to pointer, not evidence for a point. The claim that no paper has users rate their own answers 'over time' and compares a judge against that is borderline given PRISM-X, which the answer itself describes as the closest test; not counted as an error.

noreviews-q3-r2.comment: Broadest and fully accurate on everything I checked: Re-Centering Table 6 (p. 15), §6.3 (p. 9), §6.2 (p. 8), §5.2 (p. 6; κ 0.300/0.426/0.597 rounded); CUPID α 0.769 on 230 items (p. 3); LaMP-QA 73%/58%, 78%, 48%/0.94 vs 73%/0.44 (p. 7) and the original-user statement (p. 10); RewardBench oracle 97.78–99.09% (p. 15) vs 75.94%, and rejected responses 'generated deliberately to avoid these criteria' (p. 4); PersonaLens Table 5; OP-Bench 0.68 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.74 for the best judge (A.3.2, p. 14); AlpsBench 73–96% (p. 4); PRISM-X r, τ, top-1 and 44.9%/7.2% (p. 18); Trust or Escalate abstention (p. 7). The Prediction-Powered Inference paper indeed has no LLM-judge experiment, and the answer says that use is by analogy. The position-bias figure quoted is the Sim-Dynamic condition only, not labelled as such. Omits 54.6%, the text/table inconsistency and the naive-simulator caveat.

nonotes-q3-r1.comment: No errors found. Checked: 54.6% (p. 8), Table 6, r = 0.90, Δ = 0.03 and −0.39, reward models about 0.3 (p. 9), κ 0.60/0.30 and 20% vs 40–60% (p. 6), PRISM-X τ 0.22, 40.1% vs 0.57, 68.8% (p. 17) and 33.8%/15.0% (p. 18), RewardBench 97.5% on 2,830 pairs (B.4, p. 17), LaMP-QA 73%/58% and judge sizes, PersonaLens (personalisation is the lowest of the six rows in Table 5), 80 items/367 ratings/three annotators (Appendix G, p. 15), the text-vs-Table 6 inconsistency (Llama-3.3-70B: 0.376 and 4.019), the naive-simulator caveat (p. 25), and Beyond Recall's 'feasible … but was not done' (§3.3, p. 23). Point 12 is stated without the r value; point 13 only for the Sim-Judgement condition; point 27 without the ~76% inferred-needs figure; point 16 without the sycophancy half. It is the only answer to catch point 10. It says it did not reread PPI and Trust or Escalate, which are named only as pointers.

errors.quote: No paper here has users rate answers to their own requests. The human raters are third parties reading a profile, so even the "human" side is a proxy
errors.paper_says: PRISM-X, which the answer itself cites, is first-party: 530 re-recruited participants each conversed with all four models blind and gave their own ratings, rankings and willingness-to-pay bids (Introduction, p. 2; §3.1 Protocol, p. 8), and the simulators are scored against those participants' own rankings (§4.1, p. 16–17).

errors.quote: both Re-Centering and LaMP-QA say the user is the only reliable judge
errors.paper_says: Only LaMP-QA says something close, and weaker: 'the most reliable evaluator is the original user who posed the question' (Limitations, p. 10). Re-Centering Humans makes no such statement; its Limitations (p. 9) say only that personalisation is subjective and that averaging collapses variation across annotators.

CUPID does give the human ceiling for this meta-evaluation: agreement between the three annotators is Krippendorff's α 0.467, 'moderate agreement' (Appendix A.1, Meta-Evaluation for Preference Match, p. 15). The judge's 0.769 is against the majority vote.

asis-q3-r1.misleading: Mildly: the conclusion (no for 'better for this person', yes for rubric checks) is sound, but saying no paper has users rate answers to their own requests hides that PRISM-X is exactly that first-party evidence, so a reader would underrate how directly the individual-level failure is established.
asis-q3-r1.comment: Numbers and pages are otherwise accurate: Table 6 (p. 15), 0.325 ceiling, PRISM-X τ 0.22 vs 0.57 and 40.1% vs 68.8% (p. 17, Fig. 8), r = 0.98–0.99, PersonaLens Table 5 (Fleiss κ 0.75), LaMP-QA 73%/58%/κ 0.726/78%/48%–73%/0.94–0.44, CUPID α 0.769 (p. 3), 54.6% (p. 8), reward models about 0.3 (p. 9), SCV 0–19% (Table 3, p. 7) and its concession in Limitations (p. 9) that LLM judges are still ahead on identifying the personalised class. The skipped-paper claim is correct. The mention of the review file is about a failed write, not evidence.
